title: “Dead Man's Curve” by Jan and Dean
text: "Dead Man's Curve" is a song by the American vocal duo Jan and Dean. Released as a single in December 1963, the song details a teen street race gone awry.
listen: Dead Man's Curve Jan and Dean

title: “Come a Little Bit Closer” by Jay and the Americans
text: "Come a Little Bit Closer" is a song by the 1960s rock and roll band Jay and the Americans. It reached number 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 on November 21, 1964, making it the band's highest-charting single.
listen: Come a Little Bit Closer Jay and the Americans

title: “A World Without Love” by Peter and Gordon
text: "A World Without Love" is a song recorded by the British duo Peter and Gordon and released as their first single in February 1964. It was included on the duo's debut album in the UK, and in the US on an album of the same name.
listen: A World Without Love Peter and Gordon

title: “Have I the Right?” by The Honeycombs
text: "Have I the Right?" was the debut single and biggest hit of the English band the Honeycombs. It was composed by Ken Howard and Alan Blaikley, who had made contact with the Honeycombs, a London-based group, then playing under the name of the Sheratons, in the Mildmay Tavern in the Balls Pond Road in Islington, where they played a date.
listen: Have I the Right? The Honeycombs

title: “Don't Let the Rain Come Down (Crooked Little Man)” by The Serendipity Singers
text: "Don't Let the Rain Come Down" is a folk music single, and the debut recording of the Serendipity Singers in 1964. The song was based on the English nursery rhyme "There Was a Crooked Man".

title: “Baby Love” by The Supremes

title: “Let It Be Me” by Betty Everett & Jerry Butler

title: “You Don't Own Me” by Lesley Gore

title: “Walk On By” by Dionne Warwick
text: "Walk On By" is a song written by Burt Bacharach and Hal David for singer Dionne Warwick in 1963. Warwick's recording of the song peaked at number six on the US Billboard Hot 100 and number one on the Cash Box Rhythm and Blues Chart In June 1964 and was nominated for a 1965 Grammy Award for the Best Rhythm and Blues Recording.
